reasoning: Both attempts are correct and well structured. Each keeps per-player signals with per-player keys, guards the first payload with a ready handshake, bridges the signal into the UI with useSignalState, and passes every check. A wins narrowly for three reasons: it uses --!strict throughout; the label and picker share a layout container instead of a hand-computed offset; and both the limit and the starting values live only in the shared module, while B sets its starting value inside gameplay code. B's handling of the limit (synced remaining count, label hidden until known) is equally valid.

criteria.note: Per-player signal from Charm.signal(SyncedPlayerData.Default) is created on join and dropped on leave; update copies with table.clone; the check reads data.BlocksLeft <= 0.
connect is called once and fires syncRemote to that player; addSignalsToClient uses the per-player key PlayerData-{userId} only after readyRemote; removeClient runs on PlayerRemoving.
startAsync registers setData under the matching key, then connects OnClientEvent to client.patch, then fires readyRemote, so the first full payload can't be missed.

strengths: The 50 limit is defined once, in a shared module both sides use, and the label shows a sensible value before the first sync
A separate ready remote makes sure the first full payload reaches the client
Strict typing and an easy-to-extend per-player key design
The label and hotbar share a layout container, so the label always sits just above the picker
weaknesses: Refactors more than needed (a new Hotbar wrapper, and BlockPicker no longer positions itself)
The gameplay limit lives in a data-defaults table rather than next to the code that enforces it
